name: Lateral corticospinal tract
modality: voluntary skilled movement of the limbs
summary: The main voluntary motor pathway. Pyramidal neurons of the motor and premotor cortex send axons through the corona radiata, the posterior limb of the internal capsule, the middle of the crus cerebri and the basis pontis to the medullary pyramid, where about 85–90% cross in the pyramidal decussation to descend in the lateral funiculus of the cord as the lateral corticospinal tract, ending on interneurons and, for the hand, directly on motor neurons of the anterior horn. Because the crossing happens at the cervicomedullary junction, a lesion anywhere above it weakens the opposite side of the body and a lesion below it the same side, and the accompanying signs of the neighbors (face, cranial nerves, sensation) give the level.

origin.note: Roughly a third each from the primary motor cortex, premotor/SMA and the somatosensory cortex; Betz cells contribute a small fraction of the fibers.

neuronChain.cellBody: Upper motor neuron: pyramidal cells in cortical layer V
neuronChain.synapse: on spinal interneurons and directly on alpha motor neurons (corticomotoneuronal, hand)

neuronChain.cellBody: Lower motor neuron: anterior horn cell

decussation.note: About 85–90% of fibers cross; the arm fibers cross rostral to the leg fibers, the basis of cruciate paralysis.

waypoints.note: origin in the motor cortex, somatotopic
posterior limb: face at the genu, arm anterior, leg posterior
dispersed bundles among the pontine nuclei in the basis pontis
compact tract on the ventral medulla
lateral funiculus, medial to the spinocerebellar tract; leg fibers lateral
termination on interneurons and motor neurons

termination: Interneurons of the intermediate gray and alpha motor neurons of the anterior horn at every level of the cord, most densely in the cervical and lumbosacral enlargements.

lesionEffectsByLevel.effects: Contralateral weakness following the homunculus (face and arm on the convexity, leg medially), often with cortical signs; seizures
Dense contralateral hemiparesis of face, arm and leg with no cortical signs (pure motor stroke)
Contralateral hemiparesis with ipsilateral third nerve palsy (Weber)
Contralateral hemiparesis with ipsilateral VI or VII palsy (Millard–Gubler, Foville); bilateral: locked-in
Contralateral hemiparesis sparing the face with ipsilateral tongue weakness (medial medullary)
Ipsilateral upper motor neuron weakness below the level (Brown-Séquard)

pearls: Upper motor neuron signs (spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski, clonus) mark the tract; lower motor neuron signs mark the anterior horn or nerve
Weakness with a cranial nerve palsy on the opposite side is the brainstem; with a sensory level and no face involvement, the cord
Fine independent finger movements are the first and last casualty of corticospinal lesions because the direct corticomotoneuronal connections serve them

somatotopy: Cortex: leg medial, arm and face lateral. Internal capsule: face anterior (genu), then arm, then leg. Crus: face medial, leg lateral. Cord: arm fibers medial, leg fibers lateral within the tract, so an expanding central cord lesion hits the arms first and extrinsic compression the legs first.

bestView.label: posterior limb of the internal capsule

imaging.normalAppearance: The tract is followed on the HCP1065 mesh in this atlas from the motor cortex through the capsule, crus, pons and pyramid. Wallerian degeneration after a stroke makes it T2-bright and atrophic along its whole length below the lesion; in ALS it is symmetrically T2-bright in the posterior limb and crus.

pathology.finding: T2 hyperintensity and atrophy of the ipsilateral capsule, crus and pyramid weeks after a large hemispheric infarct.
Bilateral symmetric T2/FLAIR hyperintensity of the corticospinal tracts from the corona radiata to the brainstem with precentral iron on SWI.
